c. How Much Can Courts Proceduralize Informal 
Rulemaking?
The court-driven addition of more procedural burdens to informal 
rulemaking, exemplified by preceding cases like State Farm and Nova 
Scotia, is said to be hmited by the Supreme Court’s ruling in Vermont 
Yankee Nuclear Power Corp. v. Natural Resources Defense Council, 435 
U.S. 519 (1978). To understand Vermont Yankee, we must begin with some 
background on developments that led to the case. 
>
Section 553(c) does not require an agency to provide any opportunity 
*
for oral communications, and the typical rulemaking proceeding does not 
include a hearing of any recognizable kind. The lack of opportunity for oral 
exchange generally, and specifically the effective foreclosure of cross- 
examination, have long had their critics, see Robinson, supra; William F. 
Dixon, Rulemaking and the Myth of Cross-Examination, 34 Ad miN. L. Rev.
389 (1982). During the 1970s, Congress appeared sympathetic. While 
consciously avoiding requirements for formal rulemaking, it directed 
agencies to provide some opportunity for oral presentation in connection 
with a number of rulemaking statutes. These included the Occupational 
Safety and Health Act, 84 Stat. 1590 (1970), codified at 29 U.S.C. §§ 651, 
655; the Consumer Product Safety Act, 86 Stat. 1212 (1972), codified at 15 
U.S.C. §§ 2056, 2058; the Safe Drinking Water Act, 88 Stat. 1662 (1974), 
codified at 42 U.S.C. § 300g—1(d); the Energy Policy and Conservation Act,
89 Stat. 923 (1975), codified at 42 U.S.C. §§ 6295, 6306; the Clean Air Act 
Amendments of 1977, 91 Stat. 776-7, codified at 42 U.S.C. § 7607(d); the 
Federal Mine Safety and Health Amendments Act, 91 Stat. 1291 (1977) 
(since superseded by the Mine Improvement and New EmArgAncy 
Response (MINER) Act of 2006, Pub. Law No. 109-236); and the 
Endangered Species Act Amendments, 92 Stat. 3764 (1978), codified at 16 
U.S.C. § 1533. Some statutes went so far as to mandate some opportunity 
for interested persons to question or cross-examine witnesses. Magnuson- 
Moss Warranty-Federal Trade Commission Improvements Act, 88 Stat. 
2183 (1975), codified at 15 U.S.C. § 57a(c)(2); Toxic Substances Control Act,
